summary: Guests can send absolute-form HTTP requests to different hosts
description:
### Summary

Wasmtime's implementation of `wasi:http` in the `wasmtime-wasi-http` crate did not check that the value a guest passes to `set-path-with-query` on an outgoing request is actually a path. Absolute-form values such as `http://other.example/x` were accepted and written verbatim as the request target of the HTTP/1.1 request line, while the connection and the `Host` header used the authority the guest set with `set-authority`:

```
GET http://other.example/x HTTP/1.1
host: allowed.example
```

Wasmtime only connects to the authority the guest set, and any sort of request filtering based on host is done by the authority the guest set as well. However, RFC 9112 requires a server receiving an absolute-form target to ignore `Host`, so if the allowed authority is a forward proxy or a gateway that honors absolute-form targets, it forwards the request to `other.example`. A guest may then reach hosts the embedder did not have visibility into or allow. Both `wasi:http@0.2` and `wasi:http@0.3` are affected, including guests run with `wasmtime serve` and `wasmtime run -S http`.

### Impact

This issue can cause hosts using the `wasmtime-wasi-http` crate to erroneously have requests sent to hosts that are otherwise explicitly disallowed in filtering policies.

### Patches

Wasmtime 36.0.18, 48.0.6, and 49.0.3 have all been released which fixes this issue.

summary: `wasi-http`: Request with long url before query parameter crashes host
description:
### Summary

A guest sending a request with `?` occurring after byte 65535 in the url string can cause a panic in the host. This occurs because wasmtime-wasi-http's dependency on `http` was at a low enough bound to encounter [`http` issue 855](https://github.com/hyperium/http/issues/855): the byte index of `?` is stored as a `u16` which can overflow. If indexing at the wrapped value results in an invalid character offset then the `http` crate will panic when trying to split at that offset. The fix to this issue is to require a more recent `http` crate version which includes the fix.

Guests can use the WASI http `set-path-with-query` to a string of any length and `wasmtime-wasi-http` will pass it unmodified to the `http` crate, so this is a guest-controlled panic in the host. It affects versions of wasmtime >= 46 with the WASIp3 interface and >= 48 with the WASIp2 interface. Earlier versions aren't affected because the panic in `http` happen in a thread and wasn't re-raised in the host.

### Patches

Patches are present in main and in 48.0.6 and 49.0.3.

### Workarounds

No known workarounds.

summary: Filesystem sandbox escape when renaming symlinks with trailing slashes
description:
## Impact

Wasmtime's filesystem implementation provided in the `wasmtime-wasi` crate contained a bug which allowed guests to escape their filesystem sandbox and read/write external directories. Guests provided write-access to any directory within their sandbox could move any directory on the filesystem the host process could access into their sandbox, and then read and write its contents. This bug is a full filesystem sandbox escape for guests.

This bug is closely related to [GHSA-vqjp-4c8c-hfgg](https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/security/advisories/GHSA-vqjp-4c8c-hfgg). When renaming a file or directory, `wasmtime-wasi` strips a trailing slash from the source path to resolve its parent directory, but then re-appends the slash to the final path component before passing it to the `renameat` syscall. A guest could create a relative symlink pointing outside of its sandbox, for example `symlink("../outside", "up")`, and then rename `"up/"` to a path within its sandbox. The host kernel would then follow the trailing-slash symlink and move the directory outside of the sandbox into the sandbox. The fix for GHSA-vqjp-4c8c-hfgg only changed how paths are opened, not how they are renamed, so this affects all published versions of Wasmtime at the time of this advisory's publication.

This bug does not affect users on Linux or Windows, where `renameat` does not follow a symlink with a trailing slash. Users on macOS or FreeBSD, however, are affected by this issue. Only symlinks to directories can be used to escape the sandbox in this manner.

## Patches

Wasmtime 36.0.18, 48.0.6, and 49.0.3 are being released with this advisory which patches this issue.

## Workarounds

There is no known workaround for this issue. Users are recommended to upgrade to a patch release of Wasmtime that contains a fixed version of `wasmtime-wasi`.

## References

* [GHSA-vqjp-4c8c-hfgg](https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/security/advisories/GHSA-vqjp-4c8c-hfgg)
* bytecodealliance/wasmtime#14663 (the related `remove_dir` case)

summary: Overlapping string transcode in a fused adapter can panic
description:
### Summary

Wasmtime contained a bug where components containing fused adapters, or components calling components, could trigger a panic on the host in some situations where a string is transferred from one location to another. Wasmtime historically raised a trap in this situation and recent refactorings meant that this trap was no longer raised.

### Impact

The impact of this bug is that a WebAssembly guest can trigger a `panic!()` in the host through normal default execution. This is considered a denial-of-service vector in Wasmtime. The precise scenario that a trap is raised is when a same-instance component-to-component call is made which transfers a string where the source and destination alias each other. Wasmtime prior to 49.0.0 raised a trap in this situation and refactorings in 49.0.0 meant that this no longer trapped but accidentally got the point of raising a panic. The precise behavior of this operation is something still being clarified in the upstream specification, and for now Wasmtime will continue to trap as it has historically done.

### Patches

Wasmtime 49.0.3 has been released fixing this issue and restoring the historical trap.

summary: Exception tags can cause host data structures to be unaligned
description:
Wasmtime's internal `VMContext` data structure lays out its contents to match a particular input WebAssembly module and maps the module's own constructs to host data structures. A bug in this logic meant that when a module contained an odd number of tags then future internal fields were mis-aligned. A mis-aligned host structure is undefined behavior in Rust.

## Impact

There is no known way at this time this issue can be exploited. Nevertheless mis-aligned data structures are undefined behavior in Rust and can become more serious bugs as revisions of the Rust compiler and LLVM are released, for example. This advisory is being issued to notify that users should update to a patched release of Wasmtime where this undefined behavior is not present.

This advisory only affects embedders that have WebAssembly exceptions enabled, and exceptions are enabled by default in Wasmtime 47.0.0 and later.

## Patches

The fix is present in main and patch releases are made for 48.0.6 and 49.0.3.

## Workarounds

Disable exception support in the CLI via `-W exceptions=n` or the API via `Config::wasm_exceptions(false)`.

summary: Component-model handle tables are capped only per instance and charged to no limit
description:
### Summary

A malicious guest can drive unbounded host memory growth using only component-model resource handles, with no linear memory, no core tables, no host imports, and default configuration.

### Impact

Each guest `resource.new` allocates a slot in the owning component instance's host-side handle table. Allocation is bounded only by a per-table cap and is charged to no `ResourceLimiter` or `StoreLimits`, so `-W max-memory-size` and the embedder's configured memory and table limits do not bound it. Because the cap is per component instance, a single component can exceed it many times over by instantiating a sub-component repeatedly.

## Patches

Wasmtime 49.0.3, 48.0.6, and 36.0.18 have been fixed by introducing a store-wide limit on the number of simultaneously-live component-model handles.

- Default limit: **100,000 live handles per store** (~2.4 MB of handle-table memory).
- New embedder knob: `Store::set_max_component_handles(n)` to raise or lower it.
- New CLI flag: `-S max-component-handles=N` for `wasmtime run` / `wasmtime serve`.

cwes.name: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling

summary: Panic viewing component model stream or future as the wrong type
description:
### Summary

Wasmtime may panic if host tries to read from a `StreamReader<T>` which, prior to passing through guest code, was created as a `StreamReader<U>`, where `T` and `U` are different types which both correspond to the same component model type.

### Details

It is possible for an embedder to create a stream using `StreamReader::<T>::new`, pass it to guest code, and receive it again later from guest code as a different type `StreamReader<U>` as long as both `T` and `U` correspond to the same component model type.  In this case, since the host holds both the read- and write-ends of the stream, Wasmtime will attempt to optimize reads by moving the items directly from the source buffer to the destination buffer without any lifting or lowering.  However, in order for that to work, the source and destination item types must match, and this was ensured by comparing the Rust `TypeId`s and panicking if they didn't match.  That should have been an error rather than a panic.

### Impact

Embedder code which creates streams using `StreamReader::new`, passes them to guest code, and accepts streams back from the guest using a different Rust-level item type may be affected.

summary: Wasmtime may not properly enforce async-entrypoint requirement
description:
### Summary

A `Store` in Wasmtime has insufficient checks when mixing async-style and sync-style calls into WebAssembly when the store otherwise does not require async calls to be performed. This can lead to arbitrary host code being suspended and moved across threads, which can be unsound with `!Send` local variables for example, or internal panics within the runtime itself due to unexpected scenarios being hit.

## Impact

This bug can lead to panics within the runtime in certain scheduling situations. This bug can additionally lead to unsoundness in arbitrary host code if `!Send` variables, such as `Rc<T>`, are present on the stack. Wasmtime typically statically disallows this at compile time, but the missing checks for this issue failed to check this condition.

This bug is not controllable from guest-code, however, and requires the host to manually re-enter WebAssembly from host functions via sync-style APIs while originally calling WebAssembly via async-style APIs. This vulnerability requires this specific 
shape of embedder code to be written or otherwise this is inapplicable. If an embedder doesn't use async at all, then they are unaffected.

All preexisting versions of Wasmtime after 42.0.0 are affected by this issue.

## Patches

Wasmtime 48.0.6 and 49.0.3 have been released fixing this issue.

## Workarounds

If the store otherwise requires async entrypoints to be used, such as an async host function being defined, will correctly require all entrypoints to use async.

summary: Stack overflow dropping a long chain of recursive types
description:
### Impact

Guests can trigger a crash in the host by defining a long chain of types which causes the host to stack overflow when removing the top level type from the type registry. This was caused because dropping one type can remove all references to an inner type and trigger a recursive call to drop that inner type which generates a stack who's depth is controlled by the length of the type chain. The dropping logic was originally protected against this guest-controlled recursion by converting it into an iterative loop, but recursion was accidentally introduced in Wasmtime 42.0.0. So all versions >= 42.0.0 are affected.

### Patches

The fix is present in main and patch releases are made for 48.0.6 and 49.0.3.

### Workarounds

There are no known workarounds.

summary: Panic when pending calls are run after a trap
description:
### Summary

Wasmtime may panic if additional event loop tasks are allowed to run after the store is poisoned due to a trap and left in an inconsistent state.

### Details

When Wasmtime generates a trap error due to e.g. misbehaving guest code or improper use if embedder APIs, it may leave the `Store` in an inconsistent and "poisoned" state.  In most cases, attempting to continue to use that `Store` will result in more errors, but in this case, when a call that was started earlier is allowed to proceed after the trap, it was possible to trigger an assertion failure which panicked instead.

### Impact

Embedder code which continues to use a `Store` after an earlier operation involving that store has errored may be affected.

summary: Panic when invoking an async-lifted function via `call`
description:
### Summary

Calling an async-lifted guest export function using `component::Func::call` led to a host panic.

### Details

The `Func::call` function in affected versions of Wasmtime contained an assertion that the guest export to be called did not use the `async` ABI option, resulting in a panic otherwise.  This was left over from an earlier time when Wasmtime had a `async_support` config option, which the `component_model_async` option depended on, and which, when enabled, caused `Func::call` to return an error immediately, making the assertion unreachable.  Since then, the `async_support` option and corresponding guards were removed, but the assertion remained.

### Impact

Embedder code using `Func::call` to call arbitrary component exports may be affected.

summary: Yielding in a component start function can lead to a host panic
description:
### Summary

When Wasmtime ran a component start function which called an async-lowered import followed by a call to the `thread.yield` intrinsic function, it triggered a panic on the host side.

### Details

In the aforementioned scenario, the runtime code responsible for resuming a guest thread became confused about which state the thread was in, mistakenly overwriting and dropping the internal fiber belonging to that thread.  Because Wasmtime-managed fibers must be disposed of explicitly before they are dropped, and because this one wasn't, the `drop` function panicked.

### Impact

Embedder code which instantiates arbitrary components may be affected.

summary: Panic on erroneous call-to-host from guest realloc call
description:
### Impact

The `may_leave` flag is not cleared when calling `realloc` for the lowering of `stream` or `future` results. A Wasm module may then trigger a host panic during `realloc`. The root cause of this is that certain states of the `Store` are invalid when Wasm is calling into the host and these states are not properly enforced when running `realloc` because it should not be able to call back into the host. Some examples of ways a panic could be triggered are by cancelling the `read` that is currently being lowered or calling `waitable-set.wait` on a set that is already being waited on. All wasmtime versions >= 46.0.0 (or older versions which enabled `component-model-async`) are impacted.

### Patches
The fix is present in main and patch releases are made for 48.0.6 and 49.0.3.

### Workarounds
There are no known workarounds.

summary: Host panic when component `call_async` is cancelled under some conditions
description:
### Summary

The `Future` returned by `TypedFunc::call_async` may trigger a panic when dropped under certain circumstances.

### Details

The `Drop` implementation for the `Future` returned by `TypedFunc::call_async` includes code to clean up and possibly cancel its associated guest task.  However, in the scenario where that task has not yet started (e.g. due to guest-imposed backpressure or because the runtime event loop has a backlog of pending work to finish first), the code responsible for finding and removing any work items associated with that task was only looking in one of several places in which those items might be found.  Consequently, it returned an error prematurely if it couldn't find any such items which was escalated via a `Result::unwrap` to a panic in the `Future`'s `Drop` implementation.

### Impact

Embedder code using `call_async` and potentially dropping the returned `Future` before it has yielded a result may be affected.

summary: Out-of-bounds zero-length stream writes can panic
description:
### Summary

Wasmtime's API bindings to component model streams contained a bug where a panic could be triggered when the guest performed a zero-length read or write using an out-of-bounds address. The component model specification says that in this situation the address is not validated, which Wasmtime adheres to, but this lack of validation wasn't accounted for when Wasmtime later indexed into guest linear memory and this could trigger a panic. 

### Details

This bug only affects users of the `Direct{Source,Destination}` APIs, specifically the `remaining` method. These APIs are used by Wasmtime's implementation of WASIp3 which means that all embedders providing access to Wasmtime's WASIp3 implementation are affected.

### Impact

All embedders which provide access to Wasmtime's WASIp3 implementation in the `wasmtime-wasi` crate are affected, as well as embedders which use the `Direct{Source,Destination}::remaining` function directly.

summary: Rooting for GC values live across `try_call` may be missing, causing GC heap corruption
description:
## Impact

When compiling a Wasm module that uses GC references, a GC reference that is live across a `try_call` may, in certain conditions, not be properly rooted. If the callee causes a garbage collection, that reference may become stale or dangling, causing further issues including GC heap corruption or other incorrect execution.

Every Wasmtime version with GC and exceptions is affected by this issue. Both GC and exceptions are on-by-default in Wasmtime v47 and above.

## Patches

The fix is present in main and patch releases are made for 48.0.4 and 49.0.2.

## Workarounds

Disable exception support in the CLI via `-W exceptions=n` or the API via `Config::wasm_exceptions(false)`.

summary: WASI preview 0 implementation of `poll_oneoff` circumvents fuel consumption
description:
## Impact

The WASI preview 0 implementation of `poll_oneoff` in `wasmtime-wasi` causes the host to do perform work which is `O(n)` in the number of subscriptions passed without consuming fuel or checking if fuel has run out. This exposes a DOS attack vector where a guest can perform long-running computations which ignore fuel limits. Systems using the `wasmtime` cli are affected because WASI preview 0 is enabled by default. Systems using `wasmtime` as a library are unaffected unless they explicitly enable WASI preview 0 via [`p0::add_to_linker_async`](https://docs.rs/wasmtime-wasi/latest/wasmtime_wasi/p0/fn.add_to_linker_async.html) or [`po::add_to_linker_sync`](https://docs.rs/wasmtime-wasi/latest/wasmtime_wasi/p0/fn.add_to_linker_sync.html)

The root cause is that the WASI preview 1 implementation of `poll_oneoff` does a fuel check, but the preview 0 version goes through an adapter which mutates each subscription before calling the WASIp1 version (and doesn't do its own fuel check).

WASIp1, WASIp2, and WASIp3 are all unaffected because they either properly consume fuel or don't support this API.

## Patches

The fix is present in main and patch releases are made for 36.0.17, 48.0.4 and 49.0.2.

## Workarounds

Disable WASI preview 0 support in the cli via `-Spreview0=n`.

summary: Excessive allocated memory on the host when guests don't have stdio
description:
### Impact

The `wasmtime-wasi` crate contained a bug where the `write-zeros` method on a specific type in the crate, `SinkOutputStream`, permitted an unlimited-size allocation on the host. This type is used by default for `WasiCtx`s that are created and represents a guest that doesn't actually print anything via stdout/stderr to the host. The `write-zeroes` method in the WASIp2 implementation for this type ended up not limiting the allocation made of a buffer-of-zeros to write.

This bug is related to GHSA-852m-cvvp-9p4w where the fixes applied for that advisory were intended to limit the size of host allocations, but the fix was incomplete for this specific stream and situation. Specifically the limitations previously allowed up to the size of the `check-write`-limit, but for `SinkOutputStream` the limit was previously unlimited.

This bug only affects embeddings which don't configure stdout/stderr streams. Configured streams have their own limits typically which would prevent this large allocation, but unconfigured streams use `SinkOutputStream` which allows an unlimited-size allocation.

### Patches

This issue has been fixed in Wasmtime 36.0.17, 48.0.4, and 49.0.2. All other previously published versions of Wasmtime are vulnerable and users are recommended to upgrade.

### Workarounds

Affected embeddings can work around this by specifying a custom implementation of `OutputStream` which returns a limited value from `check_write`. Embeddings can also fix this by updating a patch release, too.

cwes.name: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling

summary: Wasmtime wasi:http implementation panics with a zero timeout supplied
description:
### Impact

Wasmtime's implementation of `wasi:http` for both WASIp2 and WASIp3 contained a bug where when a 0 timeout was specified for the between-bytes-timeout request option this would trigger a panic on the host. The duration from the guest was forwarded directly to a Tokio API, a dependency of Wasmtime's `wasi:http` implementation, which is documented as panicking when a 0 duration was pased to it. A guest-triggerable panic on the host is considered a denial-of-service vulnerability in Wasmtime.

This bug affects any user of the `wasmtime-wasi-http` crate in Wasmtime when the `default-send-request` Cargo feature is enabled, which is enabled by default. Embedders which do not use Wasmtime's implementation of `wasi:http` are unaffected.

### Patches

Wasmtime 48.0.4 and 49.0.2 have been released which fix this panic by clamping the timeout duration to 1 nanosecond.

### Workarounds

There is no known workaround for this issue at this time and it's recommended that users upgrade or change their embedding to not provide `wasi:http` APIs.

summary: Mis-typed WebAssembly tag imports can lead to GC heap corruption
description:
### Impact

Wasmtime contained a bug where validation of WebAssembly components which instantiate a core module importing a WebAssembly tag was not implemented correctly. This bug meant that Wasmtime could accept an invalid component which is not sound. Specifically modules were allowed to import tags with a subtype of the original tag's type, which is not allowed by the WebAssembly specification.

This bug then enabled guests to mis-type the payload of an exception object which can lead to GC heap corruption. Wasmtime's GC heap is implemented to be resilient to corruption but this is nevertheless a bug to fix. Wasmtime is not 100% bug-free in the face of a corrupt GC heap at this time hence this advisory being issues. Wasmtime may panic in certain operations when the GC heap is corrupt, so users are recommended to update.

This bug only affects users when the WebAssembly exceptions proposal is enabled, which is on-by-default starting in Wasmtime 47.0.0.

### Patches

Wasmtime 48.0.4 and 49.0.2 have been released which fix this validation error and correctly rejects ill-formed components.

### Workarounds

There is no known workaround for this issue at this time and it's recommended that users upgrade or change their embedding to disable the WebAssembly exceptions proposal.

### References
_Are there any links users can visit to find out more?_

summary: Wasmtime component async-lifted callback result count is unvalidated, causing a native stack buffer overflow
description:
## Impact

Wasmtime contained a bug where it did not properly validate the return types of core functions used as component-model-async callback function, which in combination with how the runtime works can allow the guest to write up to ~16KB of arbitrary data of its choosing to the process's native stack.  Since the guest is able to write data of its choosing to the native stack, it is able to overwrite return addresses, which can then be used to pass control to arbitrary host code or crash the process. While OS features like address space layout randomization and a non-executable stack can thwart simple attempts of arbitrary code execution, it's still recommended for embedders to treat this as if it's a arbitrary code execution sandbox escape vulnerability.  

Wasmtime relies on `wasmparser` to validate Wasm modules and components and ensure they adhere to the rules established in their respective specifications. That validation serves as a first line of defence against malformed and possibly malicious guest code. In addition, Wasmtime includes a variety of assertions, type checks, and bounds checks when translating Wasm code and compiling it to native code, as well as runtime checks for conditions which can't be verified statically, to ensure that the WebAssembly sandbox guarantees are preserved. However, in this case none of those mechanisms caught the invalid components:

- The logic for validating the type signature of the callback function used for async-lifted exports in `wasmparser` v0.259.0 and earlier was incorrect, accepting invalid components as valid instead of rejecting them. Specifically: instead of asserting that the function takes three `i32` parameters and returns a single `i32` result, due to a typographic error it asserted that the function must either accept three `i32` parameters or a single `i32` parameter without checking the result type(s) at all.

- When Wasmtime used `wasmparser` to parse a component and convert it into an internal representation, it recorded the index of each callback function without asserting that the return type and arity were correct, assuming `wasmparser` had already done that. Later, when the compiler generated a host-to-guest trampoline function for invoking the callback function, it did not include a runtime bounds check that the array reserved for passing the parameters and accepting the result was large enough for the target function signature, trusting instead that the caller knew the type of the callee and had allocated appropriately. Finally, when the runtime called the callback, it allocated a return area on the stack matching the expected arity rather than the actual one, again assuming that `wasmparser` would have already rejected the component had there been a mismatch.

In short, the soundness of runtime calls to guest callback functions depended crucially on `wasmparser` correctly rejecting invalid type signatures, and though additional defense-in-depth bounds checks could have caught the overflow at runtime, none were yet in place.

## Patches

Wasmtime 48.0.4 and 49.0.2 have been released with a fix for this issue.

## Workarounds

The issue can be avoided by disabling the `component-model-async` feature, in which case Wasmtime will reject components which use any async features, including async callbacks. Alternatively, embedders may use a patched version of `wasmparser` (v1.260.0 or later) to validate components and reject invalid ones prior to passing them to Wasmtime.

summary: Guest can panic host through filesystem timestamp before the epoch on wasip3
description:
### Impact

The `wasmtime-wasi` crate's implementation of WASIp3 on Unix hosts contained a bug where a guest could abort the host process by specifying a filesystem timestamp before the Unix epoch. The root cause is that the conversion of a guest-supplied timestamp to a system-specific representation erroneously asserted that the timestamp was after the Unix epoch.

Specifically the WASIp3 `set-times` and `set-times-at` methods on `wasi:filesystem/types.descriptor` take `new-timestamp` arguments whose `timestamp` variant contains an `instant` with a signed `seconds` field, and `wasi:clocks` documents negative seconds as times before the epoch.

The implementation of WASIp1 and WASIp2 is not affected by this issue because pre-epoch timestamps cannot be represented. This additionally does not affect Windows as the system-specific conversion code handled this case correctly. WASIp3 was first default-supported in Wasmtime 46.0.0. This additionally only affects WASIp3 implementations which give a preopened descriptor to the guest with mutable access. Read-only views of the filesystem are unaffected.

### Patches

The fix is present in `main` and patch releases are made for 48.0.4 and 49.0.2.

### Workarounds

There are no known workarounds for this issue and updating is recmomended.

cwes.name: Improper Check for Unusual or Exceptional Conditions

summary: fd_readdir copies uninitialized struct padding into guest memory
description:
### Impact

Wasmtime's implementation of the WASIp1 `fd_readdir` function contained a bug where struct padding bytes on the host were erroneously copied to the guest. This mean that 3 bytes of undefined memory were leaked to the guest on each entry yielded by `fd_readdir`. These 3 bytes of host memory are whatever happened to be left behind on the host before the host's allocation took the bytes. These 3 bytes could come from either the host's stack or the host's heap. Guests cannot control which three bytes were leaked, however, and only know that three adjacent bytes of information are leaked.

This bug only affects Wasmtime's implementation of the WASIp1 API `fd_readdir` and does not affect guests using WASIp2-or-later. This bug only affects guests which actually have a preopened directory to list entries from, guests running without a filesystem are unaffected.

### Patches

This issue has been fixed in Wasmtime 36.0.17, 48.0.4, and 49.0.2. All other previously published versions of Wasmtime are vulnerable and users are recommended to upgrade.

### Workarounds

There is no workaround for this issue if WASIp1 is enabled and guests have access to a preopened directory. Affected users are recommended to update.

summary: wasmtime-wasi: guest can panic host through filesystem datetime overflow (wasip1, 2, 3)
description:
The wasmtime-wasi crate allows guest WASI programs to trigger a host panic by specifying a filesystem timestamp value where the microseconds field overflows the seconds field. The root cause is that Rust's `std::time::Duration::new` panics in the overflow case, rather than return an error.

## wasip1

The `path_filestat_set_times` and `fd_filestat_set_times` functions take a `timestamp` typed arguments `atim` and `mtim`. A host panic is exposed if the microseconds can overflow the seconds field of this struct, e.g. `Timestamp { seconds: u64::MAX, microseconds: 1_000_000_000 }`, when passed in either argument position (atim or mtim) to these functions, as long as fst_flags does not obviate the atim or mtim argument with the ATIM_NOW/MTIM_NOW flag.

## wasip2

The `set-times` and `set-times-at` methods on `wasi:filesystem/types.descriptor` take two `new-timestamp` typed arguments `atim` and `mtim` where the `timestamp` variant takes a `datetime` struct.  A host panic is exposed if the microseconds can overflow the seconds field of this struct, e.g. `NewTimestamp::Timestamp(Datetime { seconds: u64::MAX, microseconds: 1_000_000_000 })`, when passed in either argument position (atim or mtim) to these functions.

## wasip3

The `set-times` and `set-times-at` methods on `wasi:filesystem/types.descriptor` take two `new-timestamp` typed arguments `atim` and `mtim` where the `timestamp` variant takes a `datetime` struct.  A host panic is exposed if the microseconds can overflow the seconds field of this struct, e.g. `NewTimestamp::Timestamp(Datetime { seconds: i64::MAX, microseconds: 1_000_000_000 })`, when passed in either argument position (atim or mtim) to these functions.

# Patches
The fix for this issue is present the wasmtime project's main branch, as well as in the following patch releases:

36.0.16
48.0.3
49.0.1

summary: wasmtime-wasi-http: outgoing HTTP body write allows guest-driven host memory exhaustion (DoS)
description:
## Impact

`wasmtime-wasi-http` does not enforce the write allowance that `wasi:io/streams.check-write` returns for WASIp2 outgoing HTTP bodies.

A guest can call `check-write`, get the default configured `DEFAULT_OUTGOING_BODY_CHUNK_SIZE` of 1M (or whatever value the chunk size has been customized to in an embedder's own `WasiHttpHooks` impl), and then hand a much larger buffer to `write`. The `write` call will succeed for sizes larger than permitted by `check-write`, disobeying the spec's [`wasi:io/streams`, `write` precondition](https://github.com/WebAssembly/wasi-io/blob/main/wit/streams.wit) which says such a `write` must trap. Due to this behavior, each `outgoing-body` resource created by the guest (trivial by way of creating an `outgoing-request` or `outgoing-response`) can be used to hold a host allocation of at least one linear memory sized vector for the lifetime of the guest's store.

## Patches

The fix for this issue is present the wasmtime project's `main` branch, as well as in the following patch releases:
* 36.0.16
* 48.0.3
* 49.0.1

summary: Dynamic record lifting can allocate beyond the hostcall fuel limit
description:
### Impact

Wasmtime's implementation of the dynamically-typed [`Val`] API does not adequately account for the amount of host allocations performed when loading a value from a guest. This means that a guest can return a value which allocates significantly more memory on the host than the host is otherwise keeping track of. This is a hole in the mitigations applied as part of GHSA-852m-cvvp-9p4w and represents a possible denial-of-service vulnerability for hosts.

This vulnerability only affects the [`Val`] API of hosts. Hosts that use `bindgen!` and otherwise statically-typed APIs are unaffected by this issue. For hosts using [`Val`] the amount of extra memory that can be allocated on the host depends on the exact shape of the API in question but it can be at least ~100x extra memory, for example.

### Patches

Wasmtime 36.0.16, 48.0.3, and 49.0.1 have been patched for this issue. 

### Workarounds

There is no known workaround to this and users are recommended to upgrade.

### References

* [`Val` API][`Val`]
* GHSA-852m-cvvp-9p4w

[`Val`]: https://docs.rs/wasmtime/latest/wasmtime/component/enum.Val.html

summary: `call_ref` and exception `catch` can drop some fuel accounting, leading to exponential fuel amplification
description:
## Impact

When compiling with the Cranelift backend, Wasmtime's fuel accounting around `call_ref` callsites, and also around the catch (exceptional) path for calls within `try_table`s, can drop any accumulated fuel usage within the callee, resetting to the fuel-remaining before the call. This can lead to exponential fuel amplification, that is, a guest that can run for exponential time using linear fuel, effectively avoiding timeouts or regular periodic yields. This is thus a denial-of-service vulnerability in Wasmtime.

The bug requires the use of fuel (`Config::consume_fuel` or `-W fuel=N` in wasmtime-cli), which is off by default. If fuel is enabled the bug affects any configuration using Cranelift, which is the default unless Winch has been configured, and includes users of the Pulley interpreter.

The bug only affects guests that have the `call_ref` or `try_table` opcodes present. The `call_ref` opcode is part of the function-references proposal to WebAssembly, the `try_table` opcode is part of the exception-handling proposal to WebAssembly, and users can also check if they are affected in specific cases by scanning guest bytecode for either opcode. The bug is present in all versions of Wasmtime that support `call_ref`, `try_table` and fuel. `call_ref` and `try_table` have been supported by default since Wasmtime 47.0.0. 

## Patches

Wasmtime 48.0.3 and 49.0.1 have been released with fixes for this issue.

## Workarounds

Wasmtime embedders that only require periodic interruption may consider the use of epoch interruption (`Config::epoch_interruption`) instead. Epoch interruption is not deterministic as fuel is; if deterministic fuel consumption metering is required, the only workaround is an upgrade to a fixed version of Wasmtime.

summary: Guest controlled-size host heap allocation through WASIp3 streams
description:
### Impact

Wasmtime's implementation of WASIp3 contained a bug where the host would buffer a guest-specified-length buffer on the host without limit. This bug affects WASIp3 file and HTTP streams when writing. In both situations the host would unconditionally copy all of the bytes that a guest offered to the host and then buffer them up for processing. The size of this copy is not limited beyond the valid limits of the guest's linear memory.

This advisory is similar to a [previous advisory in Wasmtime](https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/security/advisories/GHSA-852m-cvvp-9p4w) and applies to new locations not previously covered there, notably WASIp3 implementations.

### Patches

This bug is fixed in Wasmtime 46.0.3 and 47.0.4. WASIp3 notably was not enabled by default in Wasmtime versions prior to 46.0.0.

### Workarounds

There is no known workaround to this and users are recommended to upgrade.

### References

* [Historical guest-controlled host allocation CVE with Wasmtime](https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/security/advisories/GHSA-852m-cvvp-9p4w)

summary: Filesystem sandbox escape when paths or symlinks contain trailing slashes
description:
## Impact

Wasmtime's filesystem implementation provided in the `wasmtime-wasi` crate contained a bug which allowed guests to escape their filesystem sandbox and read/write external files and directories. Guests provided write-access to any directory within their sandbox could then access any directory or file on the filesystem the host process could access, and guests provided read-only access to a directory in their sandbox might be able to read any contents on the filesystem depending on symlinks preexisting in the directory. This bug is a full filesystem sandbox escape for guests.

Wasmtime's filesystem sandboxing is primarily provided by the cap-std family of crates. This dependency had a vulnerability, [GHSA-hp8f-xmx4-4qrg](https://github.com/bytecodealliance/cap-std/security/advisories/GHSA-hp8f-xmx4-4qrg), which meant that when dealing with symlinks a trailing slash could be used in specific circumstances to escape the filesystem sandbox. This affects all published versions of Wasmtime at the time of this advisory's publication.

This specific bug within cap-std does not affect users using a Linux kernel after 5.6 with the `openat2` syscall. In this situation cap-std uses the `RESOLVE_BENEATH` flag which is not affected by this bug in cap-std. Users on macOS or older Linux kernels, however, are affected by this issue.

## Patches

Wasmtime 24.0.13, 36.0.14, 46.0.3, and 47.0.4 are being released with this advisory which patches this issue. The release 48.0.0 and after is not affected by this advisory.

## Workarounds

There is no known workaround for this issue. User are recommended to upgrade to a patch release of Wasmtime that contains a fixed version of `wasmtime-wasi`.

## References

* [The `cap-std` advisory](https://github.com/bytecodealliance/cap-std/security/advisories/GHSA-hp8f-xmx4-4qrg)

summary: Stores can mix up type indices between engines
description:
## Impact

Several public Wasmtime APIs allowed putting an object belonging to `Engine` B into a `Store` belonging to `Engine` A, after which internal lookups that key on raw unique-per-engine indices silently returned the wrong answer.

This bug is ***not triggerable by guest WebAssembly programs***. It requires the embedder to create two `Engine`s and mix objects between them. The `wasmtime` CLI is not affected.

The most serious consequence is a potential out-of-bounds write. Wasmtime could accidentally use a trampoline compiled for one signature with a Wasm function of a different signature. The trampoline stack allocates space for values passed between Wasm and the host, sized based on the function's signature, and then the host writes its return values past the end of the stack allocation.

The affected entry points:

* `Instance::new`, `Instance::new_async`, `InstancePre::instantiate`, and `InstancePre::instantiate_async`: These methods did not check that the given `Module` was associated with the `Store`'s `Engine` until *after* they had already registered the `Module`'s code in the `Store`, leading to potential trampoline mismatches.
* `Store::debug_register_module`, `Store::debug_register_component`, `BreakpointEdit::add_breakpoint`, and `BreakpointEdit::remove_breakpoint`: These methods failed to check that their given `Module` or `Component` was associated with the `Store`'s `Engine`, leading to potential trampoline mismatches.
* `StructRefPre::new`, `ArrayRefPre::new`, and `ExnRefPre::new`: These methods failed to check that their given type came from the same `Engine` as their `Store`, resulting in potential GC heap corruption (sandboxed within the GC heap).
* `Tag::new`: This method did not check that its given `TagType` came from the same `Engine` as its `Store`, leading to type confusion and/or panicking.

## Patches

Every public API that takes a `Store` now correctly validates the engine. Functions that returned `Result`s return an `Err(...)` when given an object from the wrong `Engine`; functions that do not return a `Result` panic when given such an object. Wasmtime versions 24.0.12, 36.0.13, 46.0.2, and 47.0.3  have these fixes.

## Workarounds

Wasmtime embedders are highly encouraged to upgrade their `wasmtime` crate dependency. Embedders using a single `Engine` for the lifetime of the process are not affected. Embedders not directly calling one of the affected methods are not affected.

If upgrading is not an option, ensure every object handed to a `Store` was created by that store's `Engine`, for example:

```rust
use wasmtime::{Engine, Instance, Module, Result, Store, ensure};

fn instantiate<T>(store: &mut Store<T>, module: &Module) -> Result<Instance> {
    ensure!(
        Engine::same(store.engine(), module.engine()),
        "module comes from a different engine than the store",
    );
    Instance::new(store, module, &[])
}
```
